/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.headline: Nvidia moves fast on succession as Colette Kress steps in
/technology/2026/nov/12/nvidia-ceo-jense.bodyHtml:
Nvidia moved quickly to name a successor, with its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, taking over as interim chief executive until a full-time replacement is named.

The move came after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia following reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two company employees.

Huang had run Nvidia tightly and managed about 60 direct reports. Internal candidates include Kress and Ian Buck, who manages the company’s AI hardware and software products. Huang’s two children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia but are in their mid-30s and relatively inexperienced. The chipmaker also announced the appointment of Harvey Jones, a tech investor and entrepreneur, as its first-ever chair.

The chipmaker’s board earlier this week appointed the leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship with Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer and Chinese citizen who is no relation to the Nvidia boss. Nvidia had previously denied anything unusual about the relationship, but that changed on Sunday when Jensen Huang admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, Lori, without referring to Alice Huang directly.

On the same day that Jensen Huang admitted having an affair, Nvidia’s board of directors announced the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has agreed to testify before US Congress.

The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the statement said.

It added that Huang had resigned as chief executive, president and Nvidia board member “effective immediately”.

Shares in the chipmaker plunged by 13% when Wall Street opened, after Huang’s departure was announced. After a partial rebound, they closed down 4.3% on Thursday, wiping more than $180bn (£135bn) off Nvidia’s value on the day and around $490bn for the week – valuing the company at $4tn.

Dan Ives, a senior US tech analyst, said the board had done what “it needed to do, which is rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him” and that the company remained ahead of its competitors.

However, Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platform Saxo UK, said Nvidia would need a “great CEO” to replace Huang.

“His technical knowledge and understanding of every last bit of product is basically unique and impossible to replicate,” Wilson said, adding nonetheless that Nvidia was well placed in terms of upcoming products and orders.

Nvidia’s board said it would consider internal and external candidates for the chief executive’s role, with Cook featuring among potential runners and riders before Trump’s intervention. Cook stepped down as chief executive at Apple in September but still has a senior executive role at the company. Rene Haas, the chief executive of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker, has also been mooted, along with Lisa Su, the chief executive of the chipmaker AMD.

Donald Trump, who had defended Huang at first as the scandal threatened to overwhelm the Nvidia co-founder, quickly moved on to potential successors on Thursday, posting on social media that he should be replaced by Tim Cook, Apple’s former chief executive and current executive chair.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump wrote, adding: “A Legend replaces a Legend!”

The law firm had directed Jensen Huang to continue to lead Nvidia as the investigation continued.

However, late on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

The report added to the pressure on Huang, as the board called a meeting late on Wednesday to discuss the chief executive’s future.

Powell has been approached for comment.

After Huang’s resignation was announced on Thursday, Reuters reported a third alleged affair. The newly uncovered liaison was another Nvidia employee, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to the news outlet. Reuters did not reveal her name.

Huang’s exit from the company he co-founded in 1993 removes a senior figure in Silicon Valley at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex. He owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company, and was worth $145bn on Thursday morning, according to Bloomberg, making him the world’s 13th richest person.

Unlike many of his contemporaries at other leading tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.

The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. It is also one of the most valuable companies on Earth, with a market cap that hit $5tn at one point last year.

Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is a businesswoman and head of the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, who US intelligence services suspect of being a Chinese asset according to multiple reports.

/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.headline: Burnham calls for media industry to 'step forward' and protect women
/news/2026/nov/12/russell-brand-accused-.bodyHtml:
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the media industry needs to “look at itself” and “step forward” to protect women and girls following Russell Brand’s rape conviction and allegations of sexual misconduct made against the comedian David Walliams in an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

Brand, 51, was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after being convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault at Southwark crown court in London.

Brand has now also been accused of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, according to a report.

The comedian is accused of having sex with a woman without her consent and then apologising afterwards, an investigation by the Times and the Sunday Times said.

The newspapers also alleged the comedian continued having sex with another woman after she asked him to stop because he was hurting her.

The Times reported that a woman said she had an on-off relationship with the actor in the late 2000s after a professional meeting at his London home.

On one occasion, she said they were in bed together when he moved to initiate sex. Having noticed he was not wearing a condom, she said she asked him to stop.

She told the Times: “And then he was very close, on top of me, and sort of pushing – but I knew he didn’t have a condom on and I said: ‘No, stop,’ and I started to sort of try and move. And … that wasn’t happening.”

The woman added she decided at that moment that “I’m not going to fight” because “who knows what he could do”.

After the alleged incident, she said Brand apologised to her in person and by text message. “I justified it in my head by saying to myself: at least he admitted it.”

Another woman who encountered Brand when she was queueing to meet him with a friend in 2007 aged 19 said she told him during sex: “It’s painful”, according to the report.

She alleged he would not stop, adding: “And then it gets worse and it’s really painful. And I say ‘stop’ and he doesn’t stop.”

The woman claimed he said afterwards: “Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn’t want to do.”

Brand is also accused of misconduct by a fan, then in her late 20s, who met him after he performed at The Chapel venue in San Francisco in 2013, who claimed he “manhandled” her and forced his hand down her trousers, telling the Times: “I didn’t resist. I just sort of let it happen.”

Another woman, then in her mid-twenties, said Brand approached her in 2005 at a music festival and told her: “Please I just need to have sex with you, I will pay you.”

According to the Times investigation, Brand is also accused of misconduct by a woman who was in her late 20s when she won a BBC 6 Music competition and was invited as a guest on his show in 2006.

After seeing each other sporadically for the next year, she claimed the comedian told her to lick a toilet seat at his house and “got angry” when she refused, adding: “[He] seemed pissed off that I wouldn’t let him humiliate me.”

Another woman, who worked at a London venue Brand visited regularly in 2015, said a member of Brand’s staff told her there: “Russell wants you” and said: “He’s in the disabled toilets”.

She said when she went in the lights were off and Brand claimed he wanted toilet paper, but grabbed her when she went to hand it to him.

The new allegations could not be reported until his criminal case ended to avoid prejudicing proceedings. The Times reported that “extensive steps” were taken to corroborate the claims and that none of the sources were paid.

The newspapers reported that Brand was approached for comment via legal representatives after his conviction on Monday. His lawyer reportedly said he would consider “injunctive relief” but did not send any response to the allegations despite being given additional time and an agreed deadline passing. Brand has previously denied wrongdoing and claimed all his relationships were consensual.

Walliams has denied the allegations. Brand’s lawyer was contacted for comment.

/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/12/uk-ministers-l.headline: Ministers move to close NDA loopholes that silence harassment victims
/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/12/uk-ministers-l.bodyHtml:
Ministers are looking at ways to change the law quickly to expand protections that stop non-disclosure agreements being used to cover up harassment or discrimination in the wake of the allegations about David Walliams.

This could involve extending measures that mean an NDA cannot be used this way to silence an employee so that it also applies to others, such as freelancers or volunteers.

Following an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News, which said Walliams used his power and status to prey on young women for sex, there have been reports that NDAs were used by an employer to silence at least one woman connected to him.

Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and a top-selling children’s author, denies any wrongdoing.

The Employment Rights Act bars NDAs being used to stop employees disclosing possible harassment or discrimination, and a recent government consultation looked at the idea of extending this protection more widely.

Such moves are expected to be speeded up after a planned meeting next week between Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, and representatives from TV and film – both of which rely heavily on freelance or contract staff – as well as publishing and sport, to discuss possible new protections.

“We are very much in the space of looking at areas that we can change quickly and without legislation if there are loopholes,” one government official said. “It is still early but extending these protections beyond employees is definitely the sort of thing we are looking at.”

Under other existing legislation, NDAs cannot be used to stop victims or witnesses of crime from giving information to certain specified bodies, for example police or regulators.

Another possible change could extend this protection so that people could speak about crimes to anyone, including the media.

Campaigners had already been pushing for greater safeguards against NDAs before the allegations about Walliams, or the conviction of Russell Brand, who was jailed on Monday for rape and sexual assault.

Zelda Perkins, a former PA to Harvey Weinstein who broke an NDA that barred her discussing the now-jailed Hollywood producer’s predatory behaviour, and has since become a leading campaigner against their misuse, said she hoped the government, led by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), would be galvanised by the Walliams allegations.

“I have great confidence that [DBIST] are trying to create the best possible version of this,” she said. “But extending protections over harassment and discrimination beyond employees is absolutely key, and this is something where we need to keep up the pressure. The last couple of weeks have really highlighted the issues around this.”

Answering questions on Wednesday in the Commons, Nandy agreed with a Conservative question about the need to stop NDAs being abused, saying they were “central” to the problem of enforced silence.

“I am working closely with colleagues at MoJ [Ministry of Justice],” she said. “I’ve discussed this issue with them over recent days. This will be part of the conversation that we have with the creative industries when I convene the roundtable next week.”

Separate moves, albeit in the slightly longer term, are likely to lead to a law change so that any adult who has penetrative sex with a child aged under 16 would automatically be charged with rape.

This was recommended by Louise Casey’s review into sexual abuse grooming gangs published last year, following concerns that some gang members had been able to face less serious charges by claiming they had consent for the abuse.

Lady Casey has called for swifter action to protect children and young people from high-profile men, and has urged ministers to change the law to close such loopholes.

An official said: “This was happening anyway, but there is pressure to move quickly in the light of this week. We are looking at it, but we don’t yet know when it might happen.”

/uk-news/2026/nov/12/woman-18-admits-mur.headline: Kayla Smith admits murdering Leeds teenager Chloe Watson Dransfield
/uk-news/2026/nov/12/woman-18-admits-mur.bodyHtml:
An 18-year-old woman has pleaded guilty to the murder of a teenage girl who was stabbed to death during a planned fight over a young man.

Chloe Watson Dransfield, 16, was attacked by Kayla Smith, 18, after going to the latter’s home with her boyfriend Blake Dowling in Leeds, West Yorkshire, a court heard.

Smith had pleaded guilty to manslaughter but denied murder. She then changed her plea to guilty on the second day of her trial at Leeds crown court on Thursday.

Dowling, 18, who took Chloe to the house, and Archie Rycroft, 20, who followed Smith to the fight on 28 March, are also charged with murder and manslaughter and their trial will continue. They both deny the charges against them.

The judge, Mr Justice Cavanagh KC, said he would sentence Smith when the trial concluded, adding the only sentence he could give was life imprisonment but he would need to set the minimum term she must spend in custody.

The trial previously heard Dowling had been in a relationship with both Chloe and Smith and “knew of the bad feeling between the two females”, although they had never met in person before the fatal attack.

Dowling’s mother told the court Smith was “jealous and obsessed” over her son’s relationship with Chloe.

The prosecution said Chloe and Smith had argued over the phone the previous evening, with Smith threatening to “stab her” several times.

Prior to the attack, Dowling was with Chloe and spoke to Smith on the phone, who was at her grandfather’s house in Austhorpe, east Leeds, with Rycroft.

The court heard a friend of Chloe’s who was on FaceTime with her said she heard Dowling answering his phone and heard Smith screaming: “Blake, I’m gonna smash your head in … you better not be with no girls … Chloe better not be there.”

When Chloe said she was there, the witness heard Smith say: “I’m gonna stab you in your throat.”

The two love rivals agreed to fight and Dowling booked a taxi to take Chloe to Smith’s home.

Giving evidence on Thursday, the friend said that as Chloe was on the way to Smith’s house she told her she was “off to get the fight that I’ve wanted for ages”.

Gill Batts KC, defending Dowling, asked what she thought the fight would entail. The witness replied: “Just themselves, nothing else,” meaning there would be no weapons.

The court was shown CCTV and video doorbell footage which showed Smith emerging from the annexe in her grandfather’s garden holding a knife.

Rycroft followed Smith as she left the property to fight with Chloe who was heard shouting “come on big girl”, and was then seen running back to the annexe with Rycroft after the stabbing.

Chloe, who had been stabbed five times in the neck and back, bled to death.

Prosecutor Mark McKone KC said Rycroft was accused of murder “by walking with Kayla Smith to the fight and by trying to film Kayla Smith using violence and by providing support to her, if needed”.

He added Dowling knew Smith wanted to stab Chloe and by booking the taxi “played a part in organising the violence, assisted and encouraged Kayla Smith by taking Chloe to the scene for the purpose of fighting”.

Smith’s grandfather, Geoff Smith, called for an ambulance 37 minutes after the stabbing and was seen by a neighbour performing CPR on Chloe.

The jury heard Chloe was taken by ambulance to hospital but was pronounced dead at 6.40am.

When police arrested Smith and Rycroft, the prosecution said they were “laughing and joking” with two of their friends and using nitrous oxide in front of officers.

McKone said Dowling denied knowing that Chloe would be caused really serious harm, while Rycroft said he followed Smith out of curiosity and did not see that she had a knife.

The trial continues.

/world/2026/nov/13/ukraine-war-briefing-.headline: Peace talks to widen to include Europe, Kushner says
/world/2026/nov/13/ukraine-war-briefing-.bodyHtml:
• Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries, Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said late on Thursday, after meeting Russian president Vladimir Putin. “This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner said later on X. “We are also working toward what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people with their families.”

  • After the Moscow meeting, Kushner and Witkoff flew to Ireland to attend a European summit and meet Zelenskyy, who said he was pleased at the prospect of European participation in talks and said he hoped the agenda would include steps towards a ceasefire and de-escalating the conflict. “We decided that we will work on an agenda about any kind of de-escalation, some kind of ceasefires,” Zelenskyy said after meeting the US envoys. “I hope that we will have such agenda,” he said.

  • Kushner told Putin Washington had detected what he called “a big change” on the European side and was confident that expanding peace talks to include the Europeans would not hinder progress. Putin said Moscow had always been open to talking to the EU about Ukraine, but signalled serious outstanding differences. “As far as the Europeans are concerned, we have never been opposed to engaging in dialogue with Europe, and we have never broken off that dialogue. It was they who broke off the dialogue with the Russian Federation,” he said. “We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the US administration as a whole, to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” said Putin.

  • Steve Witkoff said Europe’s planned role at the next meeting was “a very important moment” because European countries are partners whose participation matters to Washington and Moscow alike, even as Putin’s own comments underlined how difficult the negotiations could become, given sharp differences between Moscow and European capitals over the way the war should end. “The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment because they are our partners and it’s important to us that they take part,” Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.

  • Putin warned Europe not to send peacekeeping troops into Ukraine in the event of a peace deal, saying it was a “continuation of war”. Putin also refused to soften his territorial demands and said Washington must work with its European allies to understand if they want peace or war in Ukraine.

  • Zelenskyy said new restrictions were affecting the US-made satellite communications Kyiv uses on the battlefield, and that he found the US approach of discussing a new European security order with Russia “a bit strange”. Earlier on Thursday, he said disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service had affected the entire frontline and Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine. Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service, and Ukraine suffered similar disruptions last month. “So far we know very little (on the Starshield restrictions). But some things are already clear: if someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then it tells us where things are going,” he said. SpaceX declined to comment.

  • The talks took place as the conflict between the two countries continued. A Russian drone strike killed two people in the northern Ukrainian region of Sumy, Governor Oleh Hryhorov said on Telegram late on Thursday, while in Rivne in the north-west, five people were injured after a Russian drone hit an apartment building, a local Ukrainian official said on Telegram early on Friday. In Russia’s Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, a man was killed and another four injured in a drone attack, local officials said on Telegram on Thursday. Meanwhile, Ukrainian agricultural company Kernel Holding said on Thursday it had suspended operations at all its oilseed extraction plants following a series of Russian attacks on its facilities.

/us-news/2026/nov/12/trump-jd-vance-iran.headline: US-Iran hostilities ease as Trump declares war 'effectively over'
/us-news/2026/nov/12/trump-jd-vance-iran.bodyHtml:
The US has not carried out massive strikes against Iran for several months, and Iran has not launched barrages of ballistic missiles against US bases and allies in the region, even as Donald Trump’s latest announcement effectively normalises a stalemate. The US has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports but has mostly reopened the strait of Hormuz to marine traffic, including crude oil shipments.

Trump said last week that he was downplaying the possibility of new strikes on Iran and called the war “effectively over”.

Gulf state leaders have lobbied him not to resume the war, Trump said.

During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran, and that an escalation was not needed.

“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters during a briefing at the White House, which took place shortly after he met with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

Donald Trump has said that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered JD Vance, who had spearheaded recent efforts to restart negotiations with Iran, to focus on domestic politics instead.

In a post to his social media site on Thursday, Trump said he was redirecting the vice-president to focus his “complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S”.

On Thursday Trump appeared to shut down the negotiations, redirecting Vance to focus on domestic issues and downplaying the need for a final deal.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Vance had reportedly been talking to intermediaries in Iran and Qatar about restarting negotiations to end the war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. Iran responded by closing access to the strait of Hormuz, which led to a steep increase for the cost of fuel around the globe.

The decision effectively sidelines Vance from the main foreign policy challenge of his vice-presidency. He had publicly distanced himself from the war, and in April he led a US delegation to Islamabad to negotiate an end to it. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff have also been involved in negotiations.

Axios last week reported that Vance was speaking “almost daily” with Sheikh Mohammed; Pakistan’s army head, Asim Munir; and other mediators. Several weeks ago he also sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, to resume direct negotiations.

Vance last week blamed the conflict for the historic rout dealt to Republicans in the midterm elections.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said after the midterms in a lengthy post on X. “The president himself said so last night.”

Trump has since doubled down on launching the war on Iran, admitting that it drove up fuel prices but repeating his frequent assertion that it was needed to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

/environment/2026/nov/12/china-rules-out.headline: China's renewable capacity overtakes coal as emissions start to fall
/environment/2026/nov/12/china-rules-out.bodyHtml:
China’s renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.

Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.

Even so, China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.

The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.

“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.

“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.

The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.

That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.

The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.

No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

/world/2026/nov/13/fan-bay-plotting-room.headline: Hidden second world war 'brain' bunker beneath Dover's cliffs opens to public
/world/2026/nov/13/fan-bay-plotting-room.bodyHtml:
It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.

The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. This acted as a “brain” for a gun battery that was used to defend Dover and attack German ships in the Channel, according to Jon Stewart, who led the excavation project for the National Trust.

Stewart was the first person to enter the bunker when it was rediscovered in 2017 after it had been secretly mothballed in 1957 and classified until 1981 owing to its military importance.

“It was a Tutankhamun moment for a conflict archaeologist,” he said. “We had done all this research on the people who had served there, and then suddenly you’re standing in their office. It was an exciting moment.”

The plotting room and the artillery it controlled can be directly traced to Churchill. Soon after his “fight them on the beaches” speech, he visited the Kent coast and was alarmed to observe enemy ships passing through the strait of Dover unchallenged.

At the same time, Dover was on the frontline of a Britain facing regular bombardment by enemy guns in occupied France.

In a July 1940 memo Churchill wrote: “We have to fight for command of the straits by artillery, to destroy the enemy batteries and fortify our own.”

He ordered the most advanced technology to be used and demanded weekly updates on progress on Dover’s new defences. The guns were ready within 100 days and the plotting room bunker was completed 64 days later.

“The guns were known around here as Churchill’s pets,” Stewart said.

Physical traces of the urgency of the construction were still visible at the site, said Stewart. He pointed to the rough openings through the walls and floors for the cabling. Contemporary accounts describe how the equipment was installed before drawings governing its layout were available.

The plotting room housed a 1.8-metre-long electromechanical computer known as a fire direction table. It was used to calculate the position of moving ships when shells hit and to send firing instructions to gun crews.

Stewart said the discovery of the plotting room reminded him of the rescue of Bletchley Park, the codebreaking site in Buckinghamshire, in the 1990s. “We didn’t know about it then, but now it’s all part of our national consciousness,” he said. “The plotting room is a new hidden history.”

He added: “We tend to think of plotting tables as glamorous Wrens [members of the Women’s Royal Naval Service] pushing around markers on a map as they do in war films. But it’s not a map – it’s a really cutting edge electromechanical computer, and it is completely unique.”

The computer was deliberately destroyed in 1957 to stop it falling into enemy hands.

Up to 10 people at a time worked in the plotting room. Stewart is keen to make contact with anyone who had family members who served there, to help him understand how the machine worked.

“What we know about it is based on a manual and ghost markings on the floor. I would really love to hear if anybody knows if their family members served at Fan Bay because the records are scant.”

The identities of only a handful of people who operated the computer are known. They include Wallas Eaton, an actor who later appeared as Senator Ludicrus Sextus in the TV comedy series Up Pompeii, alongside Frankie Howerd.

A man named WP Bryant, a lance bombardier, was also recorded as a plotter at Fan Bay. “He was a tailor so he probably had a head for numbers,” said Stewart.

The plotting room, which from Friday can be visited via National Trust guided tours through a hatch in a field, has been preserved as Stewart and his team found it. Remnants include old newspapers found on the floor, old shoes and official notices. There is also chalked graffiti on one of the service tunnels saying “heroes fan hole Dodds and Petitt”. Stewart said Dodds and Petitt may have been involved in installing cables to the bunker.

“They were probably self-appointed heroes responsible for marshalling horrible thick cable through particularly uncomfortable tunnels,” he said.

“There’s something very special about standing in a place that has changed so little since the people who worked here left. Rather than recreate the past, we’ve carefully conserved the plotting room so visitors can experience it much as we found it, with all the marks of its history still visible. It’s a rare opportunity to discover a completely different side of the white cliffs.”
